paragraphs.heading: The chemistry of being alive
paragraphs.text: Metabolism is the whole set of chemical reactions that keep a living thing alive, all happening inside its body. The name comes from a Greek word meaning change. In a wider sense the word also covers every chemical reaction in an organism, including digestion and the moving of substances into and between cells. These reactions are sped up by enzymes, and they let organisms grow, reproduce, keep their structures in shape and respond to what is around them.

paragraphs.heading: Three main jobs
paragraphs.text: Metabolism has three main jobs. It turns the energy in food into a form cells can use for their work. It turns food into building blocks for large molecules, among them proteins, lipids, nucleic acids and some carbohydrates. And it gets rid of the wastes that metabolism produces. The amount of energy used by all these reactions together is measured as the basal metabolic rate.

paragraphs.heading: Breaking down and building up
paragraphs.text: Reactions come in two kinds. Catabolic reactions break compounds down, as when cellular respiration turns glucose into pyruvate, and they usually release energy. Anabolic reactions build compounds up, such as proteins and carbohydrates, and they usually use energy. Most of the structures in animals, plants and microbes are made of four classes of molecule: amino acids, carbohydrates, nucleic acids and lipids. Metabolism either makes these molecules to build cells and tissues or breaks them down to get energy from them.

paragraphs.heading: Pathways and enzymes
paragraphs.text: Reactions are linked into metabolic pathways: chains of steps that change one chemical into another, with a specific enzyme handling each step. An enzyme is a catalyst, something that lets a reaction go faster. Enzymes also let a cell control how fast a reaction runs, for example when its surroundings change or when other cells send signals. They can even drive reactions that need energy and would not happen alone, by pairing them with reactions that give energy off. Many proteins are enzymes.

paragraphs.heading: One creature's food, another's poison
paragraphs.text: An organism's metabolism decides which substances count as food for it and which count as poison. Some prokaryotes feed on hydrogen sulfide (H₂S), a gas that is poisonous to some animals. Yet humans and certain other mammals make tiny amounts of H₂S themselves. There it does vital work in signaling and regulation.

paragraphs.heading: Shared across life
paragraphs.text: The basic metabolic pathways look strikingly alike in very different species. The acids that act as stepping stones in the citric acid cycle turn up in every known organism, from the single-celled bacterium E. coli to huge animals like elephants. These shared pathways probably appeared early in evolution. They were likely kept because they work well.

paragraphs.heading: When metabolism goes wrong
paragraphs.text: Normal metabolism breaks down in several diseases, among them type II diabetes, metabolic syndrome and cancer. Cancer cells also run their metabolism differently from healthy cells. Those differences can point researchers to targets for treating the disease.
